questions.text:
Choose ONE science idea from the Resource Booklet:
• Science Idea One: Using genetic techniques to conserve endangered New Zealand birds
• Science Idea Two: How are glaciers affected by rising global temperatures?

For Part One, focus on these two features of science (FOS):
• the development of science ideas in response to new evidence or varied perspectives, such as Māori and Pacific knowledge systems
• linking new evidence to existing models, theories, and ideas

How does EACH feature of science contribute to the development of the science idea?
(i) How does the development of science ideas in response to new evidence or varied perspectives contribute?
(ii) How does linking new evidence to existing models, theories, and ideas contribute?
questions.expectedAnswer: Identify how each FOS contributed to the science idea with examples from the resource
questions.markingGuide:
Achieved: Identify each FOS and outline how it contributed.

Idea One: (i) Mātauranga Māori perspectives recognise kākāpō as taonga, influencing DOC to prioritise conservation.

Scientists now include iwi in decision-making about breeding programmes.

(ii) DNA sequencing data was linked to existing population genetics models to identify individuals with the most genetic diversity for breeding.

Idea Two: (i) Researchers from Pacific Island nations brought new evidence about sea-level rise patterns that changed how scientists model glacier retreat timelines.

(ii) Ice-core data from Franz Josef Glacier was linked to existing climate models showing the relationship between CO₂ concentration and temperature.

questions.text: Why are these features of science important to the development of the science idea?
questions.expectedAnswer: Explain WHY each FOS was significant, giving reasons and examples from the local context
questions.markingGuide:
Merit: Explain why each identified FOS was significant.

Idea One: Including Māori perspectives is significant because iwi have centuries of observations about bird behaviour and habitats that Western science had overlooked.

This knowledge improves breeding programme success.

Linking DNA evidence to existing genetics models is significant because it helps scientists predict which pairings will produce the healthiest offspring with the greatest genetic diversity, improving long-term survival.

Idea Two: Pacific perspectives are significant because these communities observe environmental changes first-hand, providing ground-truth data that supplements satellite measurements.

Linking ice-core data to climate models is significant because it allows scientists to predict future glacier retreat rates more accurately.

questions.text: How do the two features of science work together to support the development of the science idea?
questions.expectedAnswer: Discuss how the two FOS have interacted, with detailed relationship and examples
questions.markingGuide:
Excellence: Discuss how the FOS have interacted, discussing the relationship between them and how they interact with each other.

Idea One: Mātauranga Māori provided observational knowledge about kākāpō nesting behaviours that scientists then investigated using DNA analysis, linking this new genetic evidence to existing population models.

The combination of traditional ecological knowledge and modern genetics has transformed the breeding programme — neither alone would have been as effective.

Idea Two: Pacific Island researchers provided new evidence about rates of coastal change, which prompted glaciologists to revisit their existing climate models.

By linking this local evidence to ice-core temperature records, scientists refined their predictions.

Without the varied perspectives challenging the existing models, and without the new evidence being connected to established theories, the science would have progressed more slowly.

questions.text:
For Part Two, focus on these two features of science:
• interpreting patterns and interactions
• the influence of the development and use of technology on science

(a) How does the interpretation of patterns and interactions add to the science idea?
(b) How does the development and use of technology add to the science idea?
questions.expectedAnswer: Identify how each FOS contributed to the science idea
questions.markingGuide:
Achieved: Identify each FOS and outline how it contributed.

Idea One: (a) A pattern was found between low genetic diversity and poor hatching rates in kākāpō.

By interpreting the interaction between specific genes and fertility, scientists could select better breeding pairs.

(b) The development of portable DNA sequencing devices allowed researchers to analyse genetic samples in the field, speeding up data collection.

Idea Two: (a) Scientists identified a pattern of accelerating ice loss by comparing annual glacier measurements over 50 years.

They found an interaction between ocean temperature and the rate of calving at glacier termini.

(b) Satellite imaging technology (e.g. LiDAR) allowed scientists to measure glacier thickness changes with centimetre accuracy, which was impossible with older ground-based methods.

questions.text: Why are these two features of science important to the development of the science idea?
questions.expectedAnswer: Explain WHY interpreting patterns and the use of technology were each significant
questions.markingGuide:
Merit: Explain why each FOS was significant.

Idea One: The pattern linking genetic diversity to hatching success was significant because it gave scientists a measurable indicator to guide breeding decisions.

Without this pattern, pairings would have been made at random.

The portable DNA technology was significant because it removed the need to send samples to distant laboratories, allowing real-time decision-making during the breeding season.

Idea Two: The pattern of accelerating ice loss was significant because it showed the rate of change is increasing, not linear — this changes predictions about future sea levels.

Satellite technology was significant because it provided consistent, large-scale measurements that could not be obtained by researchers on foot, covering entire ice fields simultaneously.

questions.text: How does one feature of science support the other in the development of the science idea?
questions.expectedAnswer: Discuss how interpreting patterns and technology have interacted, with detailed examples
questions.markingGuide:
Excellence: Discuss how the FOS have interacted.

Idea One: The portable DNA sequencing technology allowed scientists to rapidly generate large genetic datasets in the field.

By analysing these datasets, researchers could identify patterns between specific gene variants and fertility outcomes.

The technology made the pattern detection possible — without the rapid analysis capability, they would not have had enough data to identify the genetic interactions that guide breeding decisions.

Idea Two: Satellite imaging technology generated detailed measurements of glacier changes over decades.

By analysing this large dataset, scientists could identify the pattern of accelerating ice loss and the interaction between ocean temperatures and glacier retreat.

The technology enabled the pattern to be detected at a scale that was previously impossible, and the pattern in turn guided where to focus future technological monitoring.

questions.text:
For Part Three, focus on these two features of science:
• the influence of the development and use of technology on science
• using specific language, symbols, and conventions

How do the use of technology and specific language, symbols, and conventions contribute to the science idea?
questions.expectedAnswer: Identify how technology and scientific language/symbols/conventions each contributed
questions.markingGuide:
Achieved: Identify each FOS and outline how it contributed.

Idea One: Portable DNA sequencers allowed in-field genetic analysis, providing immediate data.

Scientific language such as 'heterozygosity', 'allele frequency', and 'inbreeding coefficient' enables researchers to communicate findings precisely.

Conventions such as pedigree charts and genetic notation (e.g. Aa, AA) help share breeding plans between institutions.

Idea Two: LiDAR and satellite instruments measure glacier volume changes.

Scientific symbols and conventions such as graphs with labelled axes (temperature in °C, ice volume in km³), standard units (ppm for CO₂), and map projections using latitude and longitude allow scientists worldwide to understand and compare the data.

questions.text:
(b) Why was each feature of science significant to the development of the science idea?

(c) How do these two features of science work together to develop the science idea?
questions.expectedAnswer: Explain significance and discuss the interaction between technology and scientific language
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Merit:
- Explain why each FOS was significant.
- Idea One: Using standardised genetic terminology allows DOC scientists, university researchers, and international conservation groups to all understand the same data.
- The technology was significant because it reduced the time between sampling and results from weeks to hours.
- Idea Two: Using standard units such as ppm and km³ allowed NZ glaciologists to compare their Franz Josef data directly with European and Antarctic datasets.
- Without this shared language, international collaboration would be difficult.

For Excellence:
- Discuss how the FOS have interacted.
- Idea One: DNA sequencing technology produces raw data that must be communicated using genetic notation and conventions.
- Without the technology, there would be no genetic data to describe.
- without the scientific language, the data from the technology would be meaningless to other scientists.
- The two features work together to ensure the science idea advances — technology generates evidence and scientific language makes it communicable.
- Idea Two: Satellite technology produces precise measurements of glacier change that are expressed using internationally agreed symbols and units.
- These standardised conventions allow NZ scientists to combine their data with global datasets, strengthening climate models.
- Technology and scientific language are interdependent — technology generates the measurements and scientific conventions ensure they are understood worldwide.
